title: Warnings and bans don't steer a writer
statement: Warnings and bans don't reliably steer a writer: some invite the error they name, exact trap lists help without removing it, unchecked bans stay advisory; change what it's given instead.
example: Adding 'be careful' warnings took a prompt's pass rate from 45% to 30%.
detail: In a prompt sweep with 20 items per variant, adding 'be careful' warnings gave a 30% pass rate against the baseline's 45%, with factual accuracy at 60% in both (`icloud-work/ML learnings/prompt_engineering_deep_dive.md`); the project's reading is that warnings without actual constraints just introduce hedging (`icloud-work/ML learnings/failures_and_false_starts.md`). Bans did no better on fine-tuned models: told not to use specific facts, one used wrong specific facts instead of right ones (`icloud-work/ML learnings/sft_v7_benchmark_postmortem.md`). Another, ordered in capitals not to write about any other topic, went on writing about the wrong topic (`icloud-work/ML learnings/stage2_postmortem_full.md`). What to change instead is the material the writer may use, the hard limits on it and how the item is built.
against: a large model mostly respected a ban on listing specific evidence; the note calls that instruction good enough for a large model and insufficient for a 14B one (`icloud-work/ML learnings/sft_v7_benchmark_postmortem.md`). a large model mostly respected a ban on listing specific evidence, and the notes conclude that an instruction good enough for a large model is not enough for a 14B one. Both cases involve one small model, and the analysis ties the failure to its weak factual memory, so the finding may not carry to larger writers (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/research/failure_taxonomy.md`); whether the later fix worked is not recorded there. The same postmortem proposes hard negatives, the model's own off-topic outputs labelled as rejected, as a fix, and the falsified run's next step pairs real sources against the model's own weakest samples; neither was measured here, and both use real outputs rather than made-up faults. none found; the comparison rests on 11 sets. the forbidden list's gain came on 20 essay items in a run that also recalibrated essay difficulty, and the bad examples' effect is a correlation across runs, not a controlled test. An earlier run of this research recorded that warnings made a writer worse (45% to 30%), and in another test a writer kept inserting a date error despite a guardrail against it (`icloud-work/aptraining/Cheater/exploits/EXPLOIT-008-dbq-7doc-generic-attrib.md`). The word list belonged to a method that was set aside after it passed 0 of 50 fresh items (`icloud-work/aptraining/Cheater/exploits/EXPLOIT-003-mcqset-phrase-anchor.md`).

evidence.quote: **Method:** test_variants.py — 9 variants, N=20 each, APUSH Unit 7
| baseline | 45% | 60% | Standard prompt |
| caution | 30% | 60% | Added "be careful" warnings |

**The "caution" variant also failed:** Adding "be careful" warnings about factual accuracy produced 30% pass rate — worse than anything. Warnings that tell the model to be careful without giving it actual constraints just introduce hedging behavior. The model starts prefacing with qualifications instead of generating confident content.

**Why it doesn't work:** The model ignores negative constraints. It has strong parametric associations (France → exploration → Protestant → Huguenots → plausible but wrong) that override the instruction. Telling the model "don't use specific facts" just means it uses wrong specific facts instead of right ones.
DO NOT write about any other topic.
**Result:** Failures persisted.

2. **The current approach (negative prompting) seemed to work on Gemini.** Because Gemini is large enough to mostly respect the "no specific evidence" instruction and has accurate enough parametric memory that when it does include evidence, it's usually right. The instruction that's good enough for a large model is insufficient for a 14B model.
